english.html: issued of it, and the cause of the accused.

notes.gloss: Satius enim esse impunitum relinqui facinus nocentis quam innocentem damnari — it is better that the crime of a guilty man go unpunished than that an innocent man be condemned.

english.html: As for the marriage, it is in the first place certain that, in doubtful things, the law wills and commands that judgment be given [for it] a; so that our interpreters say that this presumption, which one ought to take in favour of marriage, conquers and overcomes almost all the others b. In the second place, the favour of the children who are issued of this cohabitation is of great weight for rendering them entirely legitimate: for although, for the ignorance and good faith of the said de Rols, by a most equitable interpretation of our canons such children may be said and deemed legitimate c, nevertheless, if we go by the truth of the matter [unclear: the print's ſi nous ignorons, perhaps for iugeons], they are not so, being undoubtedly born of lechery and begotten of adultery d. Thirdly, the cause of the accused has at all times been so favoured that the authors of our laws often admonish us to answer for them in controverted facts, and such as admit of some doubt, and to be more inclined to deliver and absolve the accused than to condemn them e; nay, even and singularly in public and capital crimes f, in which honour and life are at stake, and even though the proofs of the plaintiff and of the accuser should somewhat surpass the proofs of the defendant g. Of which one may, with Aristotle, render two or three reasons h. The first, that it is not in the power of the defendant to plead the cause, or to come into judgment, when he sees fit, as it is in the power of the plaintiff or of the accuser to sue or to accuse at his will i; whence it may be that he, being pressed to answer, has forgotten the principal point of his defence, and of the justice of his cause. The second, because just as a pilgrim, in travelling, ought always to choose and take the surer road or path k, so in doubtful and perplexed affairs the judge ought always to embrace and follow the opinion which has less danger and peril l. And no one doubts that it is incomparably surer to leave the guilty unpunished than to condemn the inno

notes.citation: Decretals X 2.27 (De sententia et re iudicata), the last chapter (chapter not identified)
notes.gloss: In doubtful cases judgment is to be given for the marriage; the same chapter is cited again at annot-052 {b2}.

notes.citation: Panormitanus (Panorme, Niccolò de' Tudeschi) on Decretals X 4.17 (Qui filii sint legitimi), c. Transmissa (cf. X 4.17.3; number unverified)
notes.original: Panorme au c. tranſmiſ ſa. qui fil. ſint leg.
notes.gloss: The presumption for marriage prevails over almost every other.

notes.citation: Decretals X 4.17 (Qui filii sint legitimi), c. 2, c. Referente and a chapter printed ex l. not. (not identified; perhaps Ex litteris nostris or Ex tenore); the Gloss on X 4.3 (De clandestina desponsatione), c. Cum inhibitio (X 4.3.3, the Fourth Lateran Council's canon 51), at its last paragraph
notes.original: c. ij. c. refe rente, c. ex l. not. qui ſi.⟨alt:fi.⟩ ſint leg. Gloſe au. c. cum inhibitio. P. ſi⟨alt:fi⟩ nal. de clandeſt. deſpon.
notes.gloss: The last paragraph of Cum inhibitio declares the children of a clandestine marriage contracted in good faith and in ignorance of an impediment legitimate; Coras's "most equitable interpretation of our canons".

notes.citation: A Code law printed l. iij. C. ſoma t. — not identified (the title abbreviation is corrupt; perhaps Soluto matrimonio, C. 5.18, or De naturalibus liberis, C. 5.27); Decretum, D. 56, c. Si gens (cf. D. 56 c. 10, Si gens Anglorum; number unverified)
notes.original: l. iij. C. ſoma t. c. ſi gens. lvj. diſtinct.
notes.gloss: Children born of fornication and adultery are not legitimate in truth, whatever equity may deem them.

notes.citation: Digest 44.7 (De obligationibus et actionibus), l. Arrianus (cf. D. 44.7.47, Paul); Digest 50.17.125 (De diversis regulis iuris antiqui, l. Favorabiliores, Gaius); Decretals X 2.19 (De probationibus), c. Ex litteris (chapter not identified); X 2.22 (De fide instrumentorum), c. Inter (perhaps c. Inter dilectos; not identified); Liber Sextus, De regulis iuris, reg. 11, Cum sunt partium iura obscura
notes.original: l. Arrianus. D. de actio. & oblig l. fauorabiliores. D., de reg. iur. ce ex literis, d. Prob. c. inter. de fid. inſtr. c. cum ſint de re. iur. au vj.
notes.gloss: Favorabiliores rei potius quam actores habentur, defendants are favoured rather than plaintiffs; and the Sext's rule that when the rights of the parties are obscure, the defendant is to be favoured rather than the plaintiff. The print's ce is c., and d. Prob. is de prob.

notes.citation: Digest 42.1 (De re iudicata), l. Inter pares (D. 42.1.38, Paul)
notes.original: l. inter pares. D. de re. iud.
notes.gloss: When judges equal in number give differing opinions, in cases of liberty the opinion for liberty prevails, and in other cases that for the defendant.

notes.citation: The Gloss on Decretum, D. 81, c. Clerici (chapter not identified); Panormitanus on the said c. Ex litteris (as note e)
notes.original: Gloſe c. cle rici. lxxxi. di Panorme au dit c. ex liter.
notes.gloss: That the accused is favoured even where the accuser's proofs somewhat outweigh his.

notes.original: Ariſtote aux ꝓblemes. partie xxix. c. xiij.
notes.gloss: Why, when the votes are equal, the defendant is acquitted: the accuser chooses his time and comes prepared, the defendant must answer when summoned, and it is safer to let a guilty man go than to condemn an innocent — the three reasons Coras proceeds to give.

notes.citation: Digest, l. Pure, § Si nat…, under a title printed ſol. except. (not identified; perhaps De doli mali et metus exceptione, D. 44.4); Code 3.7 (Ut nemo invitus agere vel accusare cogatur), l. 1 (C. 3.7.1, the sole law)
notes.original: l. pure. P. ſi nat. D. ſol, except. l j. C. vt nem. inui. ag. vel accuſ. cog.
notes.gloss: No one is compelled to sue or to accuse against his will — the plaintiff's freedom which the defendant lacks.

notes.citation: Decretals X 5.12 (De homicidio voluntario vel casuali), c. Ad audientiam (cf. X 5.12.12; number unverified)
notes.original: c. ad audiẽ tiam. de homicid.
notes.gloss: In dubiis via est eligenda tutior — in doubtful matters the safer way is to be chosen; the canonists' source for the maxim, here the pilgrim's safer road.

notes.citation: Digest 34.5 (De rebus dubiis), l. Ubi enim (fragment not identified); the Gloss on c. 2 of a title printed de re. iu. (De re iudicata or De regulis iuris), "or in the Decretum" (aut. au Decret.; not resolved)
notes.original: l. vbĩ enim D. de reb. du. Gloſe au c. ij. de re. iu. aut. au Decret.
notes.gloss: In doubtful affairs the judge is to follow the opinion of least peril. The second citation may be the note for {n}, which has none of its own.

lines: Pour le mariage il eſt en premier lieu certain, que és
choſes douteuſes, la loy veult & cõmande faire Iuge-
ment {a}. de maniere que nos interpretes diſent que ce-
ſte preſumption qu, on doit prendre en faueur de ma-
riage, vaincq & ſurmonte preſque toutes les autres {b}.
En ſecond lieu, la faueur des enfans. qui ſont iſſus de
ceſte cohabitation. eſt de grand poids pour les rendre
entierement legitimes: car iaçoir que pour l'ignorãce
& bonne foy de ladite de Rols, par vne treſequitable
interpretation de nos canons, tels enfans puiſſent eſtre
dits & eſtimez legitimes {c}: toutesfois ſi nous ignorons
par la verité de la choſe, ils ne le ſont point, eſtans in-
dubitablement nez de paillardiſe & procreez d'adul-
tere {d}. Troiſiemement, la cauſe du preuenu à eſté de
tout temps ſi fauorable, que les autheurs de nos loix
ſouuentesfois nous admoneſtent de reſpondre pour
ceux aux faits cõtrouerſes, & qui auroyẽt quelque dou
te: & d'eſtre plus procliues à deliurer, & abſoudre les
accuſez, qu'a les condamner {e}. voire meſmes, & ſingu-
lierement és crimes publiques, & capitaux {f}, eſquels
ſ'agiſt de l'honneur & de la vie, & encores que les preu-
ues du demandeur, & de l'accuſateur ſurmontaſſent de
quelque choſe les preuues du deffendeur {g} De quoy on
peut rendre auec Ariſtote deux ou trois raiſons {h}. La
premiere, qu'il n'eſt pas en la puiſſance du defendeur
plaider la cauſe, ou venir en iugement, quand bon luy
ſemble, comme il eſt au pouuoir du demandeur, ou de
l'accuſateur agir, ou accuſer à ſa volonté {i}. dont peut
eſtre qu'il, eſtant preſſé de reſpondre, a oublié le princi-
pal poinct de ſa deffence, & de la iuſtice de ſa cauſe. La
ſeconde, car tout ainſi qu'vn pelerin en voyageant, doit
touſiours choiſir, & prendre le chemin, ou le ſentier
plus aſſeuré {k}: auſſi es affaires douteux, & perplex le
iuge doit touſiours embraſſer & ſuyure l'opiniõ qui a
moins de danger, & peril {l}. Et nul ne doute qu il ne
ſoit incomparablement plus aſſeuré, de laiſſer
impuny le coulpable, que de condamner l'inno
